title: Your mother's eyes
hookLine: We returned you to your mother so her eyes might be cooled (20:40)

lines: A BABY, A BOX, A RIVER.
cards: Musa is standing in a sacred valley, barefoot, having just been told he's a prophet and sent to Pharaoh. He asks for help: his brother Harun beside him, a tongue that speaks more easily.
And God, before sending him, does something tender. He reminds Musa of his own story, from before Musa could remember anything. A baby, a box, a river.
And a mother on the riverbank, watching it float away.

teach.b: Pharaoh was killing the baby boys of the Children of Israel. Ta-Ha says God inspired Musa's mother: put him in a chest, and put the chest in the river.
The river will throw it onto the bank, and an enemy of Mine and his will take him. To save your child, let him go, toward the very palace that wants him dead.
Another surah, Al-Qasas, says her heart was left empty, and she nearly gave the secret away. Then, verse thirty-nine: I cast love on you from Me, so you'd be raised under My eye.
The baby is taken into Pharaoh's house and loved there. But he won't nurse from any woman they bring.
His sister, who has been following the chest along the bank, steps forward and says, in Pickthall's words, "Shall I show you one who will nurse him?"
Then verse forty: "and We restored thee to thy mother that her eyes might be refreshed and might not sorrow." In Arabic, kay taqarra 'aynuha: so that her eye might be cooled.
Coolness of the eye is an old Arabic way of saying deep joy and relief.

teach.h: COOL EYES: THE TEARS OF JOY.
teach.b: One explanation in the classical dictionaries: tears of grief are hot, and tears of joy are cool.

teach.h: THAT HER EYES MIGHT BE REFRESHED.
teach.b: The Qur'an uses the phrase elsewhere too, in a prayer for spouses and children who are a coolness of the eyes.
So God, sending Musa to face Pharaoh, reminds him: you were saved, and brought back, and the reason given is a mother's grief.
Before the miracles and the staff and the sea, there was a woman by a river, and God did not leave her crying.

how: Muslims retell the story of Musa's mother as a lesson in trust and in God's care for mothers; the phrase qurrat 'ayn, coolness of the eye, is common in Muslim speech and in the du'a of 25:74 for spouses and children.

a prince of Egypt, Pharaoh's own son

s: Musa nursed from the women Pharaoh's household brought
he refused them all, until his sister offered his own mother.
God reminds Musa of this story when sending him to Pharaoh
Ta-Ha places it in the sacred valley, among favors done him before.

it means joy and relief; one classical explanation is that tears of joy are cool and tears of grief hot.

games.q: the baby in Pharaoh's house won't nurse from anyone. you're his sister, watching from nearby. what do you do?
o: stay hidden so no one suspects.
step forward: shall I show you someone who will nurse him?
run home to tell your mother to come and take him.
games.why: she offers a nurse, and Musa is returned to his own mother, so her eyes might be cooled and she would not grieve (20:40).

practice: Bring to mind a mother, your own, a grandmother, a friend with a new baby, a woman who mothered you though she wasn't your mother, or one who's grieving a child, and picture her face.
What is she carrying right now that could be lightened, even a little? If she's died, you can think of something kind to do in her name, and if you pray, you can pray for her.

wordCard.voice: Musa. Returned to his mother as a baby so that her eyes might be cooled, and she would not grieve. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: so that her eye might be cooled (20:40), the idiom for deep joy.

carryVoice: Your line: so she would not grieve. Cool eyes are eyes at rest. Day four hundred seventy-seven, done.
